review_notes: I read the whole file and compared its simp lemmas with the multilinear counterparts in Multilinear/Basic.lean. I also checked uses in Alternating/Curry.lean and Alternating/Uncurry/Fin.lean. The `norm_*` simp lemmas, the `@[simps]` LIE definitions and `norm_restrictScalars` mirror the multilinear and linear-map versions and look fine. I found no rewrite cycles. I did not run Lean, so all three findings are interface judgements, not observed simp failures. The first is the weakest, because it only concerns how the simp set is organized.

findings.problem: This `@[simp]` lemma is a definitional `rfl` unfolding of the private body of `fderivCompContinuousLinearMap`. It rewrites an unapplied composite `toContinuousMultilinearMapCLM 𝕜 ∘L f.fderivCompContinuousLinearMap g` into the multilinear derivative composed with `.pi fun _ ↦ .id _ _`. That moves the term from the alternating API into the multilinear one and adds a `.pi` of identities. The applied form is already covered by the simp lemma `fderivCompContinuousLinearMap_apply`. I found no use of this lemma outside its own declaration. It is a bridge lemma, not a normal-form rewrite, so it should not be in the default simp set.
findings.proposed_change: Drop `@[simp]` from this lemma and keep it as a plain `lemma`, to be used with `rw` or `simp [..]` when the multilinear form is wanted. The applied simp lemma `fderivCompContinuousLinearMap_apply` already gives the canonical normal form.
findings.benefit: Simp keeps `fderivCompContinuousLinearMap` terms in alternating form. They are not unfolded into a multilinear `.pi fun _ ↦ .id` composite, so goals stay readable and the simp set stays small.

evidence.excerpt:
f.fderivCompContinuousLinearMap g dg v =
      ∑ i, f fun j ↦ Function.update (fun _ ↦ g) i dg j (v j)

findings.problem: The `@[nontriviality]` attribute puts this lemma in the simp set used by the `nontriviality` tactic. That tactic reduces goals to the case where a type is `Subsingleton` or `Nontrivial`. This lemma is conditioned on `IsEmpty ι`, which is a different situation, and the equation holds unconditionally on `ι`'s emptiness only. The only use I found is an explicit `simp [fderivCompContinuousLinearMap_of_isEmpty, ...]` in Uncurry/Fin.lean. The lemma is therefore in neither the default simp set nor a useful `nontriviality` set. The default simp set would not rewrite `f.fderivCompContinuousLinearMap g` here, because the statement is an unapplied function equality.
findings.proposed_change: Either remove `@[nontriviality]`, since the explicit `simp [..]` use does not need it, or restate the lemma in applied form: `f.fderivCompContinuousLinearMap g = 0` for `[IsEmpty ι]`. With that form it could be `@[simp]`, because `IsEmpty ι` is found by instance synthesis and the RHS `0` is a strictly simpler normal form.
findings.benefit: The attribute would then match the lemma's purpose. Simp could close empty-index derivative goals without callers having to name the lemma, which is what the `n = 0` case in `alternatizeUncurryFin_fderivCompContinuousLinearMap_eq_zero` currently does.

findings.excerpt: def mkContinuousLinear (f : F →ₗ[𝕜] E [⋀^ι]→ₗ[𝕜] G) (C : ℝ)
findings.problem: This file gives `mkContinuous` the simp lemma `coe_mkContinuous` and `mkContinuousAlternating` the simp lemma `mkContinuousAlternating_apply`. `mkContinuousLinear` has no application lemma at all, even though it is defined by a `LinearMap.mkContinuous` of a `toFun x := (f x).mkContinuous ..` structure. A term `mkContinuousLinear f C H x m` therefore has no simp-normal form `f x m`. A downstream user must unfold the definition or use `rfl`. Alternating/Curry.lean uses it to define `curryLeft`, and there the application is handled by a separate hand-written `curryLeft_apply_apply` proven by `rfl`.
findings.proposed_change: Add `@[simp] theorem mkContinuousLinear_apply_apply (f : F →ₗ[𝕜] E [⋀^ι]→ₗ[𝕜] G) (C : ℝ) (H : ∀ x m, ‖f x m‖ ≤ C * ‖x‖ * ∏ i, ‖m i‖) (x : F) (m : ι → E) : mkContinuousLinear f C H x m = f x m := rfl`. I expect `rfl` to work, since the underlying function of `LinearMap.mkContinuous` is the given linear map, but I have not checked this. Optionally add the matching `mkContinuousLinear_apply` in `ContinuousAlternatingMap` form, `(mkContinuousLinear f C H x : E [⋀^ι]→L[𝕜] G).toAlternatingMap = f x`.
findings.benefit: The three constructors then expose the same simp interface. Callers and downstream definitions such as `curryLeft` get the normal form `f x m` from simp, without unfolding the definition or writing a one-off `rfl` lemma.

evidence.excerpt: ⇑(mkContinuousAlternating f C H m) = f m :=

curryLeft f x v = f (Matrix.vecCons x v) :=
